item.title: ‘You Can’t Run Your Mouth All Week,’ ‘Talking All This Fake Tough Stuff’ — Shannon Sharpe Rips Jared Verse After Browns Star Calls Out Teammates
item.description: Nov 1, 2026; Pittsburgh, Pennsylvania, USA; Cleveland Browns defensive end Jared Verse (8) walks off the field during the fourth quarter of an NFL game against the Pittsburgh Steelers at Acrisure Stadium. © Barry Reeger-Imagn Images Cleveland Browns defensive end Jared Verse criticized his teammates for not standing up for him after Pittsburgh Steelers guard Mason McCormick took him down during a point-after attempt in their Week 8 game. Verse had made fiery comments about the Steelers before the matchup, but none of his teammates came to his defense when McCormick, who was penalized, swept his legs and sent him falling awkwardly. NFL icon Shannon Sharpe also weighed in on Verse’s comments, adding to the debate among fans and analysts. Shannon Sharpe Rips Jared Verse for Calling Out His Teammates While speaking to reporters on Thursday, Verse did not mince his words about how he felt when his teammates did not back him up in a tense AFC North game in Pittsburgh. The two-time Pro Bowler admitted he did not let his teammates know he would trash-talk the Steelers, including saying the Browns intended to “make Pittsburgh ours.” “The lack of reaction by those around me upset me a lot,” Verse admitted. “A similar play happened to Derek Barnett, I think, on the next field goal, and I lost it because it was my brothers and my teammates. And when you do something like that to him, it upsets me very deeply,” he said. During Thursday’s segment of the “Nightcap” podcast, Sharpe was adamant that Verse’s off-field actions towards his teammates contributed to their reaction when he was body-slammed in Pittsburgh. “I know this ain’t the guy talking about he mad at his teammates,” Sharpe said . “I know this ain’t the same guy that didn’t show up to Deshaun Watson’s victory party that he had at his house because he said it was an hour away. That ain’t that Jared Verse. Oh, we a team. But when a teammate has a get-together, ‘I ain’t driving no hour.’ Really? Guess what, when you run your mouth, and a dude power bombs you, that ain’t got nothing to do with me.” “You out here running your mouth, talking all this fake tough stuff before the game, and then when Mason McCormick body-slams you on your head, nobody moves. Not one of your teammates stepped up.” SET YOUR LINEUPS: PFN’s Free Fantasy Start/Sit Optimizer “Not one person came over to back you up. You can’t go around picking fights. Guys in a group will pick a fight, but when they’re by themselves, they’re quieter than church mice. You ain’t got your group with you. Run your mouth now,” he added. “In the NFL, if you’re gonna talk like a big dawg, you’d better play like a big dawg. You can’t run your mouth all week and then get handled like that without your own team having your back,” Sharpe concluded. Verse was traded to the Browns as part of the blockbuster deal that saw two-time NFL Defensive Player of the Year Myles Garrett move to the Rams earlier this year. The Rams selected Verse No. 19 overall in the 202

item.title: Allan Saint-Maximin explains why Steve Bruce is the greatest manager he has ever played under
item.description: Allan Saint-Maximin and Steve Bruce Allan Saint-Maximin has been talking about the managers he has played under, including at Newcastle United. United one of the eleven clubs he has played for in his career, so far. The enigmatic winger spent four seasons at St James’ Park, the longest he has ever been at a club. His 11th and latest club is Charlotte FC who are currently fifth in the MLS Eastern Conference 2026 table after 33 matches. Allan Saint-Maximin joined them in their mid-season transfer window in July, he has scored twice and got four assists in 14 matches for the team managed by Dean Smith (formerly Aston Villa manager), who have qualified for the MLS play-offs. They have one match of the normal league season still to go but last weekend Allan Saint-Maximin was sent off at the end of Charlotte’s 4-0 victory over Orlando for grabbing his crotch in the direction of an opponent. The former Newcastle United winger spent the second half of the 2025/26 season with Lens, they were desperate to keep Allan Saint-Maximim after he helped them win the French Cup and finish runners-up in Ligue 1. ASM scoring four goals and providing three assists in 13 appearances. However, the French winger opting to move to yet another new club for a new adventure with Charlotte FC. In an interview with The Athletic , Allan Saint-Maximin saying he had offers to leave Newcastle United but turned them down because he believed he owed NUFC commitment: “They gave me everything. It’s like with your kids. You prepare everything for them. You take the poo, you clean, you do every single thing you can. And when they get to the top, they look at you like, ‘Thanks, Dad, now you can go away, I will live my life’. No, you cannot betray like this. They gave me everything and it was very important to be loyal.” Allan Saint-Maximin says he enjoyed playing under Eddie Howe at Newcastle United: “So many good players came, so we started to play better, that’s why we reached the Champions League.” However, ASM naming the best ever manager he has played under across his entire career. Allan Saint-Maximin naming Steve Bruce as his favourite manager across his whole career, as he gave him the trust and freedom to express himself: “Incredible manager but we didn’t have an unbelievable squad.” Allan Saint-Maximin though naming the Newcastle United fans as his absolute favourite, giving him his greatest memories: “I will never, ever forget them.” Allan Saint-Maximin picks the 3-3 draw with Manchester City on 21 August 2022 as his top standout NUFC match memory: “When you play against the top team, you see Guardiola down the line and you get the ball and he puts his hand on his head to be like, ‘What is this player? He’s a nightmare’. You feel something’s different. To feel the voice of the crowd when you get the ball, you feel them pushing you, you feel like you are flying. It’s something special.” The Athletic also reporting: Another notable moment was his winning goal against Oxford Unit

Matthias Jaissle was appointed by Al-Ahli on 29 July 2023, only 24 hours after ASM had signed for them. The newly promoted club then saw the new manager and winger help guide them to third place in the Saudi Pro league, in the only season Matthias Jaissle and Allan Saint-Maximin spent together.

item.title: Giants DC Dennard Wilson drops defiant truth bomb on holding his defense accountable
item.description: Denny Simmons / The Tennessean / USA TODAY NETWORK Giants DC Dennard Wilson drops defiant truth bomb on holding his defense accountable appeared first on ClutchPoints . Add ClutchPoints as a Preferred Source by clicking here . Dennard Wilson has not been shy about calling out the New York Giants ’ defense this season, and the defensive coordinator is not changing his approach as the team prepares to face the Philadelphia Eagles. Asked whether there is a danger in being so blunt publicly, Wilson did not flinch . “I think we get too caught up into not speaking the truth, right? The film doesn’t lie, and it never lies. And it’s always evidence. It’s a solid tape. And what I said in front of this podium, they’ve heard me say it from the first day they were here. So it’s nothing that they haven’t heard before,” Wilson said, via SNY. Watch sports LIVE with fuboTV (free trial) Dennard Wilson talks about holding himself and his defense accountable: "We get too caught up in not speaking the truth. The film doesn't lie…too many coaches these days are scared to have those hard conversations" pic.twitter.com/5OOKpo14dQ — SNY Giants (@SNYGiants) November 5, 2026 “It’s not calling out a specific player. It’s calling out a behavior. It’s calling out what we’re not doing collectively, because at the end of the day, it’s me as well. So if I let it slip, shame on me,” he continued. “You know, I think too many coaches these days are scared to have those hard conversations.” Wilson added that a strong bond with his players is what allows him to be so direct. “If you build a relationship and you have this bond and you have this tight-knit group, you can speak to them in a certain way and identify certain things without attacking them personally. It’s not a personal attack. It’s a behavioral attack,” Wilson said. “And that’s how I go about it, and that’s how I’ve been trained to do this since I was a young coach 20-some years ago.” Wilson made headlines last month after a Week 6 loss to the New Orleans Saints, when the Giants missed 18 tackles. He did not hold back, labeling players who do not run to the ball as “traitors to the defense” and warning that “if you don’t change the behaviors, we have to change the players.” New York bounced back with a 27-21 road win over the Houston Texans in Week 7, and the Giants enter Sunday’s matchup at 4-2-1 coming off their bye. Wilson joined John Harbaugh’s staff in January after two seasons as the Tennessee Titans’ defensive coordinator, reuniting with the coach he worked under in Baltimore. The Giants will now look to keep it rolling against an Eagles team that has dropped six straight games. Related: Giants WR Malik Nabers eases injury concerns with 3-word declaration Related: Giants’ Isaiah Likely drops ‘more the merrier’ admission on New York’s potential trades

item.title: Patrick Ngongba Sets Career High In Duke Win
item.description: DURHAM, NORTH CAROLINA - OCTOBER 20: Patrick Ngongba II #21 of the Duke Blue Devils reacts following a basket during the first half of the game against the Tennessee Volunteers at Cameron Indoor Stadium on October 20, 2026 in Durham, North Carolina. (Photo by Jared C. Tilton/Getty Images) Getty DURHAM, NORTH CAROLINA - NOVEMBER 02: Patrick Ngongba II #21 of the Duke Blue Devils dunks the ball during the first half of the game against the Army Black Knights at Cameron Indoor Stadium on November 02, 2026 in Durham, North Carolina. (Photo by Alex Halloway/Getty Images) Getty DURHAM, NORTH CAROLINA - NOVEMBER 02: Patrick Ngongba II #21 of the Duke Blue Devils jostles with Tate Laczkowski #32 and Jacen Holloway #10 of the Army Black Knights for a rebound during the second half of the game at Cameron Indoor Stadium on November 02, 2026 in Durham, North Carolina. (Photo by Alex Halloway/Getty Images) Getty WASHINGTON, DC - MARCH 27: Patrick Ngongba #21 and Caleb Foster #1 of the Duke Blue Devils celebrate during the second half against the St. John's Red Storm in the Sweet Sixteen of the 2026 NCAA Men's Basketball Tournament at Capital One Arena on March 27, 2026 in Washington, DC. (Photo by Patrick Smith/Getty Images) Getty Patrick Ngongba scored a career-high 28 points in Duke’s 113-52 win over Coastal Carolina. Throughout the game, Ngongba dominated in the paint. He used his height and size to take advantage of the smaller Coastal Carolina team. He overwhelmed them and proved to be too much for them. Patrick Ngongba: His Impressive Performance Getty DURHAM, NORTH CAROLINA – NOVEMBER 02: Patrick Ngongba II #21 of the Duke Blue Devils dunks the ball during the first half of the game against the Army Black Knights at Cameron Indoor Stadium on November 02, 2026 in Durham, North Carolina. (Photo by Alex Halloway/Getty Images) Ngongba entered halftime with 18 points; he set the tone early on and continued throughout the whole half. He ended up scoring 10 more points in the second half, giving him his career high of 28 points. He was 10/13 from the field and 6/10 from the free-throw line. He even showcased his outside shooting, going 2/3 from three-point range. He spent the whole first half around the rim, catching alley-oops and backing the opponent down. It was important for him to establish the paint game early on to dictate how the game was going to go. That put a lot of pressure on Coastal Carolina to figure out how to stop it. He was able to draw a bunch of fouls, adding even more pressure to their team. In the second half, he hit back-to-back three-pointers, showing that he is more than a paint scorer. More Than Scoring Getty DURHAM, NORTH CAROLINA – NOVEMBER 02: Patrick Ngongba II #21 of the Duke Blue Devils jostles with Tate Laczkowski #32 and Jacen Holloway #10 of the Army Black Knights for a rebound during the second half of the game at Cameron Indoor Stadium on November 02, 2026 in Durham, North Carolina. (Photo by Alex Halloway/Getty Images) Ng

Patrick Ngongba: His Impressive Performance Getty DURHAM, NORTH CAROLINA – NOVEMBER 02: Patrick Ngongba II #21 of the Duke Blue Devils dunks the ball during the first half of the game against the Army Black Knights at Cameron Indoor Stadium on November 02, 2026 in Durham, North Carolina. (Photo by Alex Halloway/Getty Images) Ngongba entered halftime with 18 points; he set the tone early on and continued throughout the whole half. He ended up scoring 10 more points in the second half, giving him his career high of 28 points. He was 10/13 from the field and 6/10 from the free-throw line. He even showcased his outside shooting, going 2/3 from three-point range. He spent the whole first half around the rim, catching alley-oops and backing the opponent down. It was important for him to establish the paint game early on to dictate how the game was going to go. That put a lot of pressure on Coastal Carolina to figure out how to stop it. More Than Scoring Getty DURHAM, NORTH CAROLINA – NOVEMBER 02: Patrick Ngongba II #21 of the Duke Blue Devils jostles with Tate Laczkowski #32 and Jacen Holloway #10 of the Army Black Knights for a rebound during the second half of the game at Cameron Indoor Stadium on November 02, 2026 in Durham, North Carolina. (Photo by Alex Halloway/Getty Images) Ngongba also had nine rebounds and a block, giving Duke a defensive presence. He didn’t have a lot of blocks, but he forced misses from all over the court. His defense may have even been more important than his offense. He has become more versatile on both ends through his time at Duke so far. Ngongba makes players change their shots at times and creates difficult shots. His ability to make a difference on both ends is way more valuable than just his scoring. He plays hard every play and never takes a play off. How He Complements the Guards Getty WASHINGTON, DC – MARCH 27: Patrick Ngongba #21 and Caleb Foster #1 of the Duke Blue Devils celebrate during the second half against the St. John’s Red Storm in the Sweet Sixteen of the 2026 NCAA Men’s Basketball Tournament at Capital One Arena on March 27, 2026 in Washington, DC. (Photo by Patrick Smith/Getty Images) Ngongba is the perfect match for the guards that the Blue Devils have. Defensively, the guards like to pressure everyone up the court, so if they get beat, Ngongba is there to block a shot or force a turnover. He gives the guards the capability to pressure without worrying if they are going to get beat. Opposing teams don’t want to drive it in on Ngongba. Offensively, Cayden Boozer, Dame Sarr, Caleb Foster, and Deron Rippey Jr. like to attack the paint. This draws the bugs to try to block their shots, which leaves Ngongba wide open for a lob. He is also a really good passer, so when he gets double-teamed in the paint, he will kick it out to whichever guard is open. They all work well together. This is a good game for Ngongba to build on going forward. Establishing dominance in the paint will open up so much more for the rest of the Duke team. He draws so much attention and commands a double team. This was a great game for him and a confidence booster heading into a juggernaut of a schedule. item.title: Will It Rain at Interlagos? Sao Paulo GP Weather Forecast Puts Qualifying Most at Risk
item.description: Weather forecast for the 2026 Sao Paulo GP says Saturday's qualifying could be affected by heavy rain. (Source: MEGA) Saturday is the day to watch the sky at Interlagos. Formula 1's official forecast for the Sao Paulo GP gives a 50% chance of rain on Saturday, November 7, most likely after 2 PM and possibly lasting into the evening. That window lands right on top of qualifying, which starts at 3 PM local time, so the session that sets Sunday's grid carries the biggest risk of the weekend. The warning is substantial. The official forecast says that "if rain does occur, it could be significant," and it adds that some streets in the city could flood and standing water could form on the track. Even without a storm, gusts could reach 50 km/h (31 mph), and strong winds will affect drivers in the braking zones. F1 WARNS OF POSSIBLE FLOODING AT INTERLAGOS Formula 1's official São Paulo GP weather forecast highlights a significant risk of rain this weekend: Friday: 30% Saturday: 50% Sunday: 40% Saturday is the biggest concern, with heavy rain possible after 2 PM local… pic.twitter.com/tyajxgaycu — Everything Formula (@evrythngformu1a) November 5, 2026 Sunday doesn't look much different either. Race day should be cool and possibly unsettled, with temperatures between 13 C and 19 C (55 F to 66 F) and a 40% chance of heavy rain and thunderstorms. Still, the timing of Saturday's threat makes qualifying the session most likely to turn out chaotic. Max Verstappen didn't hide his excitement at Thursday's press conference. The Red Bull driver, who won from 17th at Interlagos in 2024, recalled "crazy races" there, including wins from the front and from the back in the rain. "It's looking like there's a chance of rain again, so that's exciting," he said. Why Saturday Afternoon Is the Danger Zone at Sao Paulo GP Interlagos makes its own weather, and the Audi F1 team explained how this week. Two reservoirs sit on either side of the circuit and put a lot of moisture into the air, and sudden temperature shifts can help storms form. Audi has explained why the Sao Paulo GP is always at risk of being affected by rain and storms. (Source: MEGA) The track also sits on a hillside about 800 meters above sea level, which pushes damp air upward, where it cools and falls as rain. That's not just a theory. Audi pointed out that wet weather has been a major factor in qualifying here in three of the last four seasons. In 2024, a heavy storm pushed qualifying back to Sunday morning, and a year later the FIA issued a rare level 4 rain warning for Saturday. Last year's Sao Paulo GP, though, ran in dry conditions, with Lando Norris winning for McLaren ahead of Antonelli and Verstappen. However, this year could be a different story. PlanetF1 , writing on November 4, put the risk at 60% for final practice and 30% for qualifying, with Sunday's race facing a 50-60% chance. Max Verstappen's epic storm lap Brazil 2023 pic.twitter.com/OE7ZY7ZH3A — MV33Racing (@MV33Racing) November 3, 2026 Fri
item.content:encoded: Weather forecast for the 2026 Sao Paulo GP says Saturday's qualifying could be affected by heavy rain. (Source: MEGA) Saturday is the day to watch the sky at Interlagos. Formula 1's official forecast for the Sao Paulo GP gives a 50% chance of rain on Saturday, November 7, most likely after 2 PM and possibly lasting into the evening. That window lands right on top of qualifying, which starts at 3 PM local time, so the session that sets Sunday's grid carries the biggest risk of the weekend. The warning is substantial. The official forecast says that "if rain does occur, it could be significant," and it adds that some streets in the city could flood and standing water could form on the track. Even without a storm, gusts could reach 50 km/h (31 mph), and strong winds will affect drivers in the braking zones. F1 WARNS OF POSSIBLE FLOODING AT INTERLAGOS Formula 1's official São Paulo GP weather forecast highlights a significant risk of rain this weekend: Friday: 30% Saturday: 50% Sunday: 40% Saturday is the biggest concern, with heavy rain possible after 2 PM local… pic.twitter.com/tyajxgaycu — Everything Formula (@evrythngformu1a) November 5, 2026 Sunday doesn't look much different either. Race day should be cool and possibly unsettled, with temperatures between 13 C and 19 C (55 F to 66 F) and a 40% chance of heavy rain and thunderstorms. Still, the timing of Saturday's threat makes qualifying the session most likely to turn out chaotic. Max Verstappen didn't hide his excitement at Thursday's press conference. The Red Bull driver, who won from 17th at Interlagos in 2024, recalled "crazy races" there, including wins from the front and from the back in the rain. "It's looking like there's a chance of rain again, so that's exciting," he said. Why Saturday Afternoon Is the Danger Zone at Sao Paulo GP Interlagos makes its own weather, and the Audi F1 team explained how this week. Two reservoirs sit on either side of the circuit and put a lot of moisture into the air, and sudden temperature shifts can help storms form. Audi has explained why the Sao Paulo GP is always at risk of being affected by rain and storms. (Source: MEGA) The track also sits on a hillside about 800 meters above sea level, which pushes damp air upward, where it cools and falls as rain. That's not just a theory. Audi pointed out that wet weather has been a major factor in qualifying here in three of the last four seasons. In 2024, a heavy storm pushed qualifying back to Sunday morning, and a year later the FIA issued a rare level 4 rain warning for Saturday. Last year's Sao Paulo GP, though, ran in dry conditions, with Lando Norris winning for McLaren ahead of Antonelli and Verstappen. However, this year could be a different story. PlanetF1 , writing on November 4, put the risk at 60% for final practice and 30% for qualifying, with Sunday's race facing a 50-60% chance. Max Verstappen's epic storm lap Brazil 2023 pic.twitter.com/OE7ZY7ZH3A — MV33Racing (@MV33Racing) November 3, 2026 Friday’s practice is expected to give teams a dry track. The official forecast calls for mostly cloudy, dry conditions, with a 30% chance of rain mainly in the early morning and at night. Williams warned that the weather could leave teams with little representative dry running before qualifying and the race, which makes Friday's laps worth more than usual. There's no sprint this year either, so teams get a third practice session at 11:30 AM Saturday. Verstappen said the extra setup time "might be good or might be bad." If you only watch one session live this weekend, make it qualifying. Drivers Joke, but Malaysia's Wet-Weather Glitch Still Lingers The rain talk on Thursday quickly turned to software. Bruna Parreira of Globo TV asked the drivers whether they worried that the 2026 cars might run into more problems in the wet, after software issues in the rain in Malaysia. Verstappen didn't miss a beat: "I installed antivirus on my car, so I'll be fine." Max Verstappen kept the mood light over the potential software issues in wet Sao Paulo GP conditions. (Source: MEGA) He then teased Racing Bulls driver Arvid Lindblad , reminding him that both teams use the same power unit. The laughs covered a real problem from earlier this season. During the wet race in Malaysia, a power unit software bug appeared, and the race got underway only after the FIA sent teams new software about 20 minutes later. Nikolas Tombazis , the FIA's single-seater director, said he could guarantee that this specific bug wouldn't return but couldn't rule out every bug. He'd already admitted that the FIA hadn't been able to test the 2026 cars enough in wet conditions beforehand. Fernando Alonso pictured exactly where a glitch would hurt most. "Hopefully not, because that is quite steep uphill, you know, after the last corner," said the two-time champion, who added that he believes the problems were understood after Malaysia. Fernando Alonso hopes the software glitch from Malaysia doesn’t affect the cars in the Sao Paulo GP. (Source: MEGA) Not everyone sees the clouds as bad news. Alpine's Franco Colapinto said Brazil's rain always brings new chances for his team, and home hero Gabriel Bortoleto said the weather can be crazy and anything can happen at Interlagos. Mercedes may need some luck, too, since the team must beat Ferrari by three points this weekend to seal the Constructors' title. Antonelli arrives with nothing left to prove and nothing left to protect. Verstappen arrives as the man who loves this place most when it's wet. Somewhere over the lakes, a storm may be deciding who starts where.

item.title: Warriors predicted to trade Kristaps Porzingis for $27M versatile stretch-big after recent update
item.description: Warriors predicted to trade Kristaps Porzingis for $27M versatile stretch-big after recent update originally appeared on The Sporting News . Add The Sporting News as a Preferred Source by clicking here . The Golden State Warriors have an interesting situation on their hands that has nothing to do with basketball and everything to do with a health issue that has created plenty of uncertainty. Kristaps Porzingis still hasn’t returned to the team after being diagnosed with POTS. The veteran center became aware of the condition shortly after training camp began. Now, Golden State is reportedly exploring ways to move his contract through a trade. “Golden State has started exploring trade routes for Kristaps Porzingis, who is now seriously contemplating his future in basketball as he deals with recurring symptoms from the autoimmune condition termed as POTS (postural orthostatic tachycardia syndrome), sources tell ESPN," ESPN's Shams Charania posted. The Warriors are certainly in a position they didn't expect to be in this early in the season. The team has been rolling, but missing a big man is never easy under any circumstances. The Athletic’s Nick Friedell reported Wednesday that the organization doesn't expect Porzingis to return to the floor. “Warriors players/coaches seem to have moved on from the idea that Porzingis will be back with the team. They are hopeful that he can get healthy, but aren't expecting him back on the floor,” Friedell wrote. With Golden State exploring trade options, Sports Illustrated’s Joey Akeley believes a deal for Chicago Bulls forward Jalen Smith could be in play. The proposed trade would send Smith and a second-round pick to the Warriors in exchange for Porzingis and a first-round pick. “Warriors get: Jalen Smith, 2027 second-round pick (via Cleveland). Bulls get: Kristaps Porzingis, 2027 first-round pick (top-11-protected),” Akeley wrote. This deal could benefit the Warriors by bringing in a versatile frontcourt player while moving Porzingis' contract. Smith can fill multiple roles and give Golden State another inside presence when needed. Smith is playing under a contract worth approximately $27 million over its full term. He is a well-rounded player who could make an impact for the Warriors this season. item.title: Scott Parker’s dramatic West Ham return leaves him struggling for words
item.description: The former midfielder with impressive managerial promotion record began with a thrilling comeback in draw at Cardiff Three days in and Scott Parker has already lost his voice. West Ham’s head coach arrived on Tuesday, watched his side fight back from 3-0 down to draw with Cardiff on Wednesday and was struggling to make himself heard when he met the media on Thursday afternoon. “It’s like in the summer holidays,” Parker said. “You put the flip-flops on for five weeks, then you come back home and you get your shoes on. You’re in a minute, you’ve got a blister on the back of your heel. It’s the same with a throat. I’ve not shouted for a little while. All of a sudden there’s shouting and it’s a bit croaky.” Continue reading...

item.title: ‘In moments of pain, football comes together’: Spain says goodbye to Jesús de Miguel
item.description: Only 3,587 people live in his family’s village but the streets of Navahermosa were fuller yet quieter to mourn the Tenerife striker at his funeral The narrow streets of Navahermosa in La Mancha were fuller than they have ever been on Thursday afternoon and quieter too. Silence accompanied the funeral cortege as its made way from the funeral home to the parish church of San Miguel Arcángel carrying Jesús de Miguel Alameda, “Demi”, the Tenerife striker who died after an on-field collision with the Andorra goalkeeper Jesús Owono three days earlier. Only 3,587 people live in his family’s village but now they were joined by the game he loved. “We wanted to be close to his parents, his wife and daughter. In moments of pain, football comes together more than ever,” said Luis de la Fuente. The Spain manager did not say much else; there was not much else he could say, not much anyone could. These have been dark, desperate days, days when it was impossible to assimilate what has happened, and there will be more. “We will get through this together but we will need help, professional help,” the Tenerife president, Felipe Miñambres, said. Continue reading...

item.title: Concacaf revamps Gold Cup format to make tournament ‘more competitive’
item.description: Group stage to involve two groups of eight teams Change resembles model of Uefa Champions League Concacaf on Thursday announced changes to the format of the Gold Cup, the confederation’s regional championship. The move is aimed at “delivering more meaningful matches and matchups between top-ranked teams”, Concacaf said in a statement. Once the primary focus of teams in the region, the 35-year-old tournament will return for its 19th edition in 2027 having lost a bit of luster. The federation’s tweaks to the format – which center around the competition’s group stage – could help restore that. Here’s a look at the tournament, what’s at stake and what is changing. Continue reading...

item.title: Football Daily | Como turn on the style and hammer nine past out-of-focus Lens
item.description: Sign up now! Sign up now! Sign up now? Sign up now! A consistent criticism levelled at Como is that they are simply not “Italian” enough to be a bona fide Serie A club. Bankrolled by an Indonesian ciggy manufacturer, their president has helpfully likened their multi-hubbed business model to that of the Walt Disney Company. In Cesc Fàbregas they have a Spanish coach and their starting XI against Lens in Bigger Cup on Wednesday didn’t feature a single Italian. To add insult to injury, they also thrashed their hosts 9-1 in a show of outright vulgarity that will have had Serie A traditionalists gesticulating angrily. Piling on the hurt against already-humiliated opposition has never been the Italian way, unless both teams have formally agreed to it before the game kicks off. Continue reading...

item.title: Champions League review: comebacks, thrashings and a Mauritanian first
item.description: Bayern Munich and Paris Saint-Germain flexed their muscles, Manchester United fought back and an unlikely star stole the show for AEK Athens Still without the recovering Vincent Kompany, Bayern Munich are among the favorites to win the Champions League, which would be their first European title since 2019-20. René Marić’s side produced a dominant display at the Metropolitano, playing Atlético Madrid off the field in a commanding 2-0 win. Lennart Karl and Konrad Laimer made the difference, with Harry Kane providing Laimer with a fine assist in his first continental appearance since winning the Ballon d’Or. Bayern remain just outside the top eight, which guarantees automatic passage to the last 16, having won two and drawn two of their opening four matches. Continue reading...

item.title: Cristiano Ronaldo merely the latest example of a great player who couldn’t let go | Jonathan Wilson
item.description: There is no doubt his international career was an incredible one, but it would have been greater still if he had not lingered on the stage so long Nothing, perhaps, is quite so difficult for an elite sportsperson as timing their exit. It’s not easy for any person in any job to weigh the hope of having more to give with the desire not to linger beyond their usefulness, but it’s perhaps particularly hard for top athletes because unrealistic self-confidence is so essential to their success. It takes an almost unhealthy level of self-belief for anybody to make the sacrifices to get to the top, to dedicate themselves to such a precarious vocation, to overcome all the setbacks and injuries and failures. How can someone – whose whole life has been spent assuring themselves there are no odds they cannot overcome – accept that is it, that the time has come to say goodbye? The news that Cristiano Ronaldo has retired from international football brings with it, inevitably, a sadness. Sadness we will no longer see him skipping past a defender, or burying a neck-thrusting header, and sadness in that the end of the career of any great is a reminder of mortality; all things in time must pass. But there is also a sadness he timed his departure so badly. For at least three tournaments, there has been a sense of Ronaldo holding Portugal back. Continue reading...

item.title: The international break is almost here: so wave goodbye to your players, and maybe your manager | Max Rushden
item.description: What used to be a time to reset is now a time to rehire, and Michael Carrick is not the only Premier League manager looking over his shoulder Perhaps the most telling moment of Manchester United’s comeback against Roma was at the final whistle. The camera focused on Michael Carrick, who shook the hand of Gian Piero Gasperini before looking around trying to remember what you’re meant to do after a victory. The camera then cut to the director of football, Jason Wilcox, and chief executive, Omar Berrada, clapping with two of the most ashen faces you could imagine – as if it was a minute’s applause in the 87th minute for a lifelong, octogenarian fan who died peacefully in his sleep earlier in the week (most probably not at a United game but you couldn’t rule it out). Of course, there are rules about smiling when you are involved with a failing football club. Players can’t be seen to be enjoying themselves in the week after a defeat, managers have to be earnest at almost all times, apart from when a journalist’s phone goes off at a press conference – a moment of sporting hilarity on a par with a pigeon landing on Centre Court. Continue reading...

item.title: Uefa faces political flashpoint over Sevastopol’s ascent in Russian football
item.description: Promotion to third tier for Crimean club would be clear violation of governing body’s rules amid conflict in Ukraine Uefa and Fifa face a decisive test of their appetite to punish Russia’s integration of teams from illegally occupied Ukrainian territory after FC Sevastopol, from Crimea, won promotion to the country’s professional third tier. Sevastopol were declared champions of group one in Football National League (FNL) 2B, in effect Russia’s fourth division, last month and are believed to have applied for a licence to compete at the level above. Should it be granted and they proceed to FNL 2A, it would appear a violation of Uefa rules that prohibit Crimean clubs from playing in competitions organised by the Russian Football Union (RFU). The governing body would come under severe pressure to extend sanctions on European football’s pariah state, whose club and national teams are banned from competing in international tournaments. Continue reading...

item.title: ‘She can do what Beckham did’: Océane Hurtré making waves at Birmingham
item.description: WSL’s second-highest goalscorer is likened to England legend for her crossing and has earned France call-up At the conclusion of Birmingham’s warm-up, the players quietly and carefully placed their footballs into a draw-string bag. All except one, Océane Hurtré, who nonchalantly chipped hers straight into the bag from about 15 yards. It was an innocuous moment that might have escaped most onlookers at Hednesford Town’s Keys Park but it demonstrated the swagger with which she is playing. To observe the 22-year-old warming up before the 1-1 League Cup draw at Aston Villa last week was to witness a player making skills look easy, taking one touch where others took two and pulling off no-look passes. She is backing up that panache in the Women’s Super League, as the joint second-highest goalscorer with six from the promoted side’s opening eight matches. Only Khadija Shaw has scored more. item.title: Has a footballer ever run a marathon faster than James Milner? | The Knowledge
item.description: Plus: managers sacked after signing new deals, war victims commemorated on kits and the first club website (part II) Mail us with all of your questions and answers It came as no surprise to the Knowledge that James Milner had spent the early months of his retirement training for – and then running in – the New York City Marathon. Yes, the bleep test-loving former Brighton, Liverpool and Manchester City player recorded an excellent time of 3hr 9min 4sec, an average of 7min 13sec per mile. Not bad for a 40-year-old whose physique is more like that of a wrestler than a whippet. “A few years ago, I feel like I could have definitely done sub-3:00,” he said, lamenting his late-career injuries for hindering him. In 2012 we ran a column listing footballers’ fastest marathon times, with the former Leicester playmaker Muzzy Izzet leading the pack on 3hr 22min 36sec at the 2011 London Marathon. That very respectable time has now been surpassed by the Premier League’s record appearance maker, so we thought we had better take a gulp of our isotonic energy drink and run through a few more tales of football’s marathon men and women. Continue reading...

item.title: Choke of the century? Chengdu collapse sets up thrilling Chinese Super League climax
item.description: John Aloisi’s players need a point on the final day to seal their maiden title – but their form has dropped off a cliff With four games of the Chinese Super League to go, Chengdu Rongcheng needed just a point to clinch their first title. With one game to go, they still need a point. What was a formality has become a formidable task. The biggest bottle job in Asian football history is very much on and it would be as popular as it would be dramatic. The coach of the Sichuan club, the former Portsmouth and Coventry striker John Aloisi, has seen a 12-point lead over Dalian Yingbo cut to just three before Sunday’s showdowns. Whatever happens, this is a positive and thrilling end to a season that started negatively – literally – with nine of the 16 top-tier clubs kicking off on minus points. Continue reading...

item.title: Mainoo and Lacey raise the spirits but systemic change still required at Manchester United | Nick Ames
item.description: There were protests at Old Trafford and even though two academy products stood out, Michael Carrick’s future is far from safe Green and yellow balloons bobbed around the Stretford End. Tennis balls rained down on the pitch in protest at the chronic, enduringly cinematic decline presided over by Manchester United’s ownership. Then came a reminder of the humble football’s extraordinary power to bend history, minds and wills. United’s players departed victorious having somehow won the game within the game, separating themselves from the fog of unhappy context swirling on all sides and turning the second half into its own soaring, ripping story for the ages. Will it be enough to save Michael Carrick, who was once again serenaded when minds wandered from the joint scourges of the Glazer family and Jim Ratcliffe? If Aston Villa defend a shade more competently than Roma on Sunday then perhaps not. United have led their supporters, remarkable in their tenor of backing for players and head coach here, up more than enough false peaks over the past 13 years. Arguably, that is one reason for Carrick being given the job on a permanent basis. Continue reading...

item.title: ‘An absolute afterthought’: the story of the Nigeria women’s team’s fall from grace
item.description: The Super Falcons won’t be at the World Cup and with the prize money going up, they risk being left even further behind It was a historic result in Casablanca – but not in a good way. Nigeria’s 2-1 defeat against South Africa in a playoff in August meant that the Super Falcons are missing out on the World Cup for the first time. It is a crushing blow for the most decorated national side in Africa across both men and women, one that has won no fewer than 10 Wafcon titles . The journalist and lecturer Dr Victor Ademola was in Morocco the day of the defeat. “It was a very difficult evening,” he says. “Some players were visibly emotional while others appeared to be processing what had just happened. I saw players crying as they got on to the team bus while some sat alone or remained on their phones, looking very sad.” Continue reading...

item.title: Football Daily | Aston Villa, ‘unacceptable insults’ and thin-skinned clutching of pearls
item.description: Sign up now! Sign up now! Sign up now? Sign up now! When Jamie Carragher appeared as a pundit on Sky Sports Super Sunday, Football Daily was surprised he didn’t have a solicitor sitting alongside him, occasionally jotting notes on a pad or leaning over to give whispered instructions and answer “no comment” to any leading questions about Trey Nyoni starting ahead of Ryan Gravenberch. On Friday night, the former Liverpool defender was subjected to a threat of legal action from Aston Villa, who took such grave exception to some “unacceptable insults” he had rained down on them from his podcast pulpit, that they were ready to call in the heavy legal artillery and stop him from preventing their “ascension in English and European football”. Taking a leaf out of the tried-and-much-ridiculed Nottingham Forest playbook , Villa chair Nassef Sawiris appears to have eschewed contacting Carragher through the usual formal channels and instead cajoled some unfortunate junior comms staffer to make the portentous announcement on their Social Media Disgraces. Continue reading...

Taking a leaf out of the tried-and-much-ridiculed Nottingham Forest playbook , Villa chair Nassef Sawiris appears to have eschewed contacting Carragher through the usual formal channels and instead cajoled some unfortunate junior comms staffer to make the portentous announcement on their Social Media Disgraces. Continue reading...

item.title: Unai Simón caps myth-making week with another extraordinary night | Sid Lowe
item.description: Athletic’s win over Real Sociedad was culmination of six unique days for the Spain keeper after night at the Palladium For the third time in six days everyone got to their feet to hand a standing ovation to Unai Simón, dressed in all black, before the world. Named the best men’s goalkeeper on the planet, holding the Lev Yashin trophy, they had applauded him at the London Palladium on Monday night and before the game began at San Mamés, Bilbao, on Sunday. Now somewhere in the middle of it all, the ferocity of the 197th Basque derby, there was another moment, even more meaningful and more lasting, a cheer again giving way to something deeper: an appreciation for a man as well as his work closing a week that will be forever his. Which means it will be forever theirs too. Real Sociedad and Athletic Club had been doing battle for 72 minutes and it was 2-1 when Simon took off to make a save that denied Carlos Soler an equaliser and defied belief . As the ball flew off his palm, San Mamés exploded. And then it happened: never mind that Athletic still had a derby to win and a corner to defend, forget the fact that the lead was a single goal, the visitors relentless now and 25 minutes still to resist; at the stadium everyone calls the Cathedral , a place of ritual and liturgy like no other, the entire congregation, 50,092 people, started clapping. Started and did not stop. For a minute, maybe more, it was like the match that matters most didn’t matter at all, momentarily fading until it was just him and them together. Continue reading...

item.title: Premier League: 10 talking points from the weekend’s action
item.description: Marco Rose’s tactics are lifting Bournemouth, Roméo Lavia makes progress with Chelsea and Roberto De Zerbi gives youth a chance at Spurs Good defending is the mark of champions. At Anfield, where Arsenal had not won in the past 13 visits, Mikel Arteta followed the orthodoxy of locking down once his team took the lead. This time around, it proved successful. Arsenal did not allow the occasion or the stadium to get to them as they have on previous occasions. In April 2023, Granit Xhaka entangling with Trent Alexander-Arnold energised home fans previously despondent that Arsenal were 2-0 up. It finished 2-2. On Sunday, Liverpool zipped around zestfully, as Andoni Iraola requests, though the final-ball quality was lacking. That owed a great deal to the organisation of the Arsenal defence. Ahead of the last international break, Brighton set a blueprint for getting the better of Arsenal in winning 3-0 . Liverpool’s squad profile might have made a similar strategy possible though Iraola’s outfit is struggling to create chances in the same volume as Brighton or his Bournemouth team. item.title: How can playing for Manchester City fit into Marc Guéhi’s moral universe? | Barney Ronay
item.description: Club’s predicament raises interesting questions about principles, both for individuals and the Premier League I felt unbelievably ponderous. My head was made of Aztec stone. I realised I didn’t want to be with all these people. Somebody came at me, a huge individual in silver and blue. I fell at his feet and grabbed one shoe. I started untying the lace. He kicked away from me. I got up and walked off. I was exceedingly hungry. Not my words. Also not the words of the Manchester City centre-back Marc Guéhi, despite what you were thinking there. This is instead a condensed quote from the mind of Gary Harkness, existentially curious college running-back and the narrator of Don DeLillo’s great American football novel End Zone. item.title: Roster rifts, police raids and Son’s uncertain future leave South Korea at a crossroads
item.description: After a disaster World Cup, the team have continued to spiral, with tensions high between young and older players and the captain’s standing in question Son Heung-min and Cristiano Ronaldo are iconic No 7s, Premier League legends and international record-breakers. Now there is a surprising danger of them having something else in common: being a divisive presence in their national teams. On 21 October, during a parliamentary committee meeting, politician Jeong Yeon-wook put a question to acting Korea Football Association (KFA) president Lee Yong-soo, that took a story out of the sports pages and into the national conversation. “It is said that recently, within the national team squad, players have been calling him not by his name but as ‘No 7’ or ‘that person’. Do you know who that is?” Lee then replied, “Are you referring to Son Heung-min?” Jeong went on: “So it appears to be true. … It has also been revealed that the national team’s leadership is causing discord and has broken down overall.” Lee declined to comment. Continue reading...

item.title: A phone-free Yellow Wall: are Dortmund urging fans to be present or policing them?
item.description: It makes sense that sports teams want to keep influencers out of their games. The battle some clubs are waging with their fans, however, is a different dilemma By all appearances, things on the Yellow Wall seemed as they always had been. The stadium announcer hollered out the first names of Borussia Dortmund’s starting lineup and the supporters responded with their last names, tens of thousands of voices bellowing as one. Dozens of black and yellow flags waved over Europe’s largest standing terrace, a mass of faces fixed on the field beneath them. And then Signal Iduna Park, sold out with 81,365 fans, roared when Max Beier’s lone goal led Dortmund to victory over Eintracht Frankfurt last Saturday, putting the home side even on points with Bayern Munich atop the Bundesliga standings. Continue reading...

item.title: Kylian Mbappé’s China crisis shows how sensitive Mao’s legacy remains | Rebecca Bailey
item.description: Real Madrid forward was dropped by brands for comments Chinese media generally steered clear of outlining It’s been a bad start to the week for the Kylian Mbappé. The France forward missed out on joining the elite roster of Ballon d’Or winners and instead became the latest high-profile addition to a far less illustrious list – that of foreign brands and individuals charged with “hurting the feelings of the Chinese people”. The saga began when a video of the Real Madrid player making light of a meme involving him and China’s former leader Mao Zedong began spreading. Continue reading...

item.title: Lise Klaveness: ‘Certainly there are people that can challenge Infantino’
item.description: Norwegian federation president distances self from Fifa presidency but believes governing body can be reformed As the rain whips around Oslo’s government quarter, Lise Klaveness is shielding herself from the wind, trying to work out tactics. “Of course we cannot probably do everything alone, but we have a voice, we have the right to speak, we have the right to suggest, so let’s see,” she says. “We will at least try to be a spearhead.” The president of the Norwegian Football Federation wants to re-engage Fifa, and other governing bodies, on the topic of remedy. A slightly arcane aspect of human rights policy in normal times, the importance of remedy became very clear in the aftermath of the World Cup in Qatar, when the families of those injured or killed in the work that led up to the tournament were left without financial compensation after Fifa chose to direct a legacy fund elsewhere. Continue reading...

item.title: Mourinho’s plan comes together as Real Madrid relaunch with clásico statement | Sid Lowe
item.description: It was just like old times as José Mourinho ended a night at Camp Nou with a knee slide and three points José Mourinho had already done the por qu é? , the printout and the press conference no-show in under 100 days. Now he’s done a knee slide too, and in the perfect place: back where it all began and where it can all begin again. When Kylian Mbappé scored the first in the clásico on Sunday night, Real Madrid’s manager hardly moved, sitting in the shadow of the bench – but when the striker got the second to win it with time running out, that was different. Mourinho leapt into the light, throwing himself to the grass, the knees of a 63-year-old’s trousers muddy as a schoolboy’s, stuck his tongue out and pumped his fists. He does so love it when a plan comes together. To the right of him, the bench was emptying, subs joining the players in sprinting towards the south-west corner. As they leapt about, dodging the bottles thrown towards them from the end, way, way up in the furthest corner and stuck inside a glass box like a bunch of David Blaines, the small group of Madrid fans who had come were going mad. In the main stand, a thousand phones were raised. And 600 kilometres west, back in Boadilla, Thibaut Courtois was watching his teammates from the sofa at home, presumably wrapped in a blanket and cradling a cup of Lemsip. On the morning of the biggest game there is, he awoke with flu, forced to miss out. Continue reading...

item.title: The horse that ushered in Manchester United’s tragic arc | Jonathan Wilson
item.description: There’s plenty of blame to go around at Old Trafford. Like all downfalls it started with a seemingly small, unconnected moment Sign up for our free newsletter here And so here we are again, at that point as the nights draw in and Manchester United prepare to sack a manager . Autumn: season of mists, mellow fruitfulness and a crisis at Old Trafford. Sunday’s 3-0 home defeat to Bournemouth , coming on the back of last week’s 4-1 reverse against Como, made clear what many had feared from the moment Michael Carrick was given the job on a permanent basis: that he isn’t up to it. But then, who could be? When you’ve burned through a long list of managers in 13 years, it’s perhaps worth considering whether the manager is really the problem. Could some blame perhaps go to the director of football, Jason Wilcox, or the chief executive, Omar Berrada, the people making the appointments? Or perhaps to Sir Jim Ratcliffe, the cost-cutting tax exile and minority shareholder with responsibility for sporting operations? Or to the Glazer family, who plunged the club into debt with a leveraged buyout in 2005 and have since made calamitous decision after calamitous decision, reducing the most successful club in English league history to a mid-table laughing stock with a roof that leaks symbolically ? This is an extract from Soccer Desk, a newsletter from the Guardian US. Subscribe for free here . Continue reading...

item.title: Ian Holloway’s circus: why the manager’s antics are no laughing matter for fans
item.description: Swindon manager has a history of viral outbursts but fans want a united club and manager they can support In Ian Holloway’s often madcap managerial orbit, this was simply the latest in a steady succession of eccentric outbursts. Eyes bulging as he spoke, he boomed the letter “D” and promptly stabbed himself in the chest with an imaginary dagger. Next came the letter “M” alongside a blow from another invisible knife. Finally, a “W” followed by a jab to the heart. “Dead. Man. Walking,” he declared, pausing for effect between words and briefly falling into an Oscar-worthy zombie stupor. “That’s how it feels.” To an offbeat press conference genre containing seagulls following trawlers and self-proclaimed special ones, it was a crazy new entry worthy of its subsequent viral nature. Holloway at his finest. Continue reading...

item.title: Shola Ameobi: ‘I thought: how can I be most useful to Newcastle? Then the cog started turning’
item.description: From experiencing racism growing up in Newcastle to becoming a derby hero and now a member of the executive team, the former striker has been on a remarkable journey “There were times where I feared for my life as a kid, being harassed and chased by different groups of people,” Shola Ameobi says. “There were situations where I had to sprint to get away from groups of lads who didn’t like me because of what I looked like.” Ameobi is recalling growing up in Newcastle during the late 1980s and 1990s, having moved from Nigeria aged six. There were lots of moments like that. Continue reading...

item.title: James McClean: ‘Wearing the poppy was just never going to happen’
item.description: The former Republic of Ireland international on growing up in a community still reeling from the Troubles and the controversy that scarred his career “The perception of me is that, basically, I am a madman,” James McClean says calmly. “I’m outspoken. I’m a loudmouth. I’m very opinionated and I hate all things British. That’s from people who don’t know me. The reality is quite the opposite. I’m pretty boring. I go training, go home and switch off. A lot of my days are quite bland, quite basic.” McClean sounds as sane as he looks gaunt on a bleak Monday in Derry. He spent 14 years in English football and the fact that he is now at war with his own club, Derry City, can’t obscure the fact that he is the fifth-most-capped Republic of Ireland international, having played 103 times. “People define success in different ways,” he says, “but I’m the only footballer from the north of Ireland to win over 100 caps for Ireland. I played 150 Premier League games over five seasons, 800 professional games and won a lot of individual accolades. I count that as success and don’t look back with regrets.” Continue reading...

item.title: Next Generation 2021: why slow and steady sometimes wins the race
item.description: Our NextGen picks from five years ago show that breaking through early does not guarantee longevity or future success Read the full updates on our class of 2021 here and here In 2021, as every year, we picked 80 players from around the world who had a chance of making it in world football – 20 from the Premier League and 60 from the rest of the world – as part of our Next Generation series . We then follow these talented boys on their journeys for five years. Often it is almost impossible to predict how they will get on (OK, when Sid Lowe sent over Lamine Yamal in 2024 we had an inkling he might do well). The ball-playing central midfielder comes from a footballing family and academy staff believe his tactical awareness is born from growing up around the game. His father, Adam, played for Brighton and is now manager along the coast at Worthing FC, while Martin (his great uncle), Paul (his grandad), and Wally (his great grandad), all enjoyed careers as players. The youngest to play in the Bundesliga at 16 years and one day, youngest player to appear in the Champions League 17 days later, youngest goal scorer in Bundesliga 11 days after that and youngest player and youngest goal scorer for the Germany Under-21 team before he has turned 17. Continue reading...

item.title: Transfer window verdict: how every Premier League club fared
item.description: The British transfer record was equalled and one club signed no fewer than 18 players in another hectic summer Bringing in Christos Tzolis, Bruno Guimarães and Ezri Konsa was a strong start to the window but could Arsenal’s failure to sign a marquee attacker cost them in the long run? They began targeting Morgan Rogers before pivoting to Vinícius Júnior when the England forward went to Chelsea, only to end up disappointed when Vinícius signed a new deal with Real Madrid. Julián Alvarez made clear he had no intention of joining from Atlético Madrid in the final days of the window and Arsenal kept their powder dry despite sanctioning the exits of Gabriel Jesus to Barcelona and Ethan Nwaneri to Borussia Dortmund. Should Gabriel Martinelli complete his move to Al-Hilal as expected in the coming days – the Saudi Pro League window remains open – a few injuries could leave Arteta short. Ed Aarons Continue reading...

item.title: Ousmane Dembélé quietly becomes the main man after long journey to the top
item.description: The Frenchman, who has been named the best male footballer in the world by the Guardian, has benefitted from PSG’s focus on the team rather than individuals What makes a good player great, and a great player the best? This question has been occupying me since 2014, when the Guardian first asked me to contribute to its inaugural Next Generation feature . My job was to look for a France-based talent born in 1997 who could go on to have a stellar career. After a great deal of research, I narrowed it down from my shortlist of five by asking questions not about the players’ football ability, but about other attributes: resilience, adaptability, decision-making, creativity, work ethic, response to feedback and willingness to learn. Qualities we cannot see, and are harder to measure. Continue reading...

item.description: The margin may have got smaller but the brilliant Spanish midfielder makes it a hat-trick of No 1 finishes They say the best things come in threes, and Aitana Bonmatí has written herself into the Guardian’s top 100 history as the first player to finish at the top of the tree for a third consecutive year. Last year the majestic midfielder emulated her Barcelona and Spain teammate Alexia Putellas by winning for a second year running , but the 27-year-old has now gone one better, establishing herself once again at the top of the women’s game. item.title: Sign up for the Moving the Goalposts newsletter: our free women’s football email
item.description: Get our roundup of women’s football for free twice a week, featuring the insights of experts such as Ada Hegerberg and Magdalena Eriksson Join us as we delve deeper into the wonderful world of women’s football in our weekly newsletter. It is informative, entertaining, global, critical – when needed – and, above all, passionate. Written mainly by Júlia Belas Trindade and Sophie Downey , expect guest appearances from stars such as Anita Asante, Ada Hegerberg and many more. Try our other sports emails: as well as the occasionally funny football email The Fiver from Monday to Friday, there are weekly catch-ups for cricket in The Spin and rugby union in The Breakdown , and our seven-day roundup of the best of our sports journalism in The Recap . Living in Australia? Try the Guardian Australia’s daily sports newsletter Continue reading...

item.title: Sign up for the Recap newsletter: our free sport highlights email
item.description: The best of our sports journalism from the past seven days and a heads-up on the weekend’s action Subscribe to get our editors’ pick of the Guardian’s award-winning sport coverage. We’ll email you the stand-out features and interviews, insightful analysis and highlights from the archive, plus films, podcasts, galleries and more – all arriving in your inbox at every Friday lunchtime. And we’ll set you up for the weekend and let you know our live coverage plans so you’ll be ahead of the game. Here’s what you can expect from us. Try our other sports emails: there’s daily football news and gossip in The Fiver , and weekly catch-ups for cricket in The Spin and rugby union in The Breakdown . Living in Australia? Try the Guardian Australia’s daily sports newsletter Continue reading...
